title: Meditation, understanding, strength, food, water (7.6–7.10)
hook: the ladder climbs past thought to meditation, and then takes a surprising turn: toward strength, food and rain

segments.voice: Yesterday: name, speech, mind, will, thought, the first rungs of Sanatkumara's ladder. Your line was each is greater. Did you notice the intention under your words? Day three hundred fifty-four.

If you were drawing a spiritual ladder, you'd probably make it climb from the body toward the mind, from the earthy to the airy. Lower things at the bottom, higher things at the top. Sanatkumara's ladder starts that way. Name, speech, mind, will, thought, each more inward. Then, today, it reaches meditation, the most inward step yet. And right after that, it does something nobody expects. It climbs toward a strong arm, a meal, and a rain cloud.
screen: `A LADDER FROM BODY TO MIND.` → `TODAY: MEDITATION.` → `THEN A STRONG ARM, A MEAL, A RAIN CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Greater than thought, Sanatkumara says, is meditation, dhyana. And his picture is beautiful. The earth meditates, as it were. The sky meditates, as it were. The waters, the mountains, gods and people, all meditate, as it were. Think of a mountain at dusk, utterly still. That stillness is what he means. He adds that people who achieve greatness seem to have a share of it, while small-minded people are quarrelsome and gossiping. Greater than meditation is understanding, vijnana: by it we know the Vedas, right and wrong, this world and the next. Then the turn. Greater than understanding is strength. One strong person, Sanatkumara says, can make a hundred people of understanding tremble. The earth stands by strength; the mountains stand by it. Greater than strength is food. Go without eating for ten days, and even if you live, you can't see or hear or think or understand. Remember Shvetaketu's fast? Same point. Food returns, and so do they. Greater than food is water. When the rains fail, people grow sick with worry about food; when the rains are good, they're glad. The earth, the sky, the mountains, people, animals, grass and trees, he says, are all just water in solid form. So what's going on? Why does the ladder climb into the body? One way to read it: Sanatkumara isn't ranking spirit over matter. He's asking what each thing depends on. Understanding depends on strength; strength on food; food on rain. The ladder climbs by asking what holds this up. And it keeps climbing.
screen: `THE EARTH MEDITATES, AS IT WERE.` · `UNDERSTANDING, THEN STRENGTH.` · `TEN DAYS WITHOUT FOOD.` · `EARTH AND MOUNTAINS: WATER, MADE SOLID.` · then, large: `WHAT HOLDS THIS UP?`

segments.voice: Today's practice meditates the way a mountain does. Sit, and let your body settle like rock: heavy, still, supported by the ground. Don't try to do anything. A mountain doesn't try. Let the breath move on its own, like weather passing over a peak. Thoughts can come and go like clouds. You are just sitting, as the earth and the sky and the waters sit, meditating, as it were. The bell holds the time.
Meditation. Dhyana, the rung above thought: the stillness of earth, sky and mountains. Above it, understanding, strength, food and water.
Your line: the ladder climbs. Today, pick one thing you rely on, and ask what holds it up, and what holds that up. Day three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Dhyana, meditation, is practiced across Hindu traditions, from Vedanta to yoga, where it is the seventh limb of Patanjali's eight; teachers often describe it with images of stillness like a mountain or a lamp in a windless place.

fork.setup: you're on Sanatkumara's ladder. you've reached understanding. what does he say is greater?
fork.reveal: strength. then food, then water. the ladder climbs by asking what holds each thing up.

original.note: Sanskrit dhyāna: meditation, steady contemplation. dhyāyatīva pṛthivī: the earth meditates, as it were.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list ranking spiritual things above physical ones.
what it means: a ladder of dependence. understanding rests on strength, strength on food, food on rain.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 7.6–7.10, dhyana, vijnana, bala, anna, apas. the ladder continues through heat, space, memory and hope to prana (7.15).

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.6 (dhyana: the earth meditates, as it were)

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): 7.10.1 lists earth, sky, mountains, gods, people, animals, plants etc. as water made solid, not food by name; the teach, its screen head and the match pair now follow the text.
7.6.1: those who attain greatness 'have a share of meditation's reward', while small people are quarrelsome, slanderous, abusive; paraphrased. Confirm.
7.9.1: ten days without food (the fast in 6.7 was fifteen); both stated correctly. Confirm.
The 'ladder of dependence' reading is interpretive, offered as 'one way to read it'. Confirm.
howItsDone: dhyana as the seventh limb in Yoga Sutras 2.29; the windless-lamp image is Bhagavad Gita 6.19.
